1.vraag: How do I set my frustration aside at the handover?
1.kort: The handover is a brief moment for your child. It isn’t the time to talk things through. Keep it short, friendly and practical.
doen: Think of one sentence beforehand, for example: ‘Hi, here’s the bag. Have a lovely weekend.’
Breathe out slowly before you arrive.
Save everything else for a message in the app.
Look at your child, not at the other parent.
Take a moment for yourself after the handover.
zeg: “Hi. Here’s the bag with the football kit. See you Sunday.”
“I’d rather talk about that later in the app.”
liever: “We still need to talk about…”
“You’re late AGAIN.”
1.onthoud: Your child picks up on the tension. A calm handover helps your child, even when it takes a lot out of you.
1.kind: A short, friendly moment at the door brings calm to {kind}.
1.kindKort: A friendly door means calm for {kind}.

2.vraag: What do I do if the other parent starts an argument at the handover?
2.kort: You don’t have to respond, and you don’t have to win. It’s fine to end the conversation calmly.
doen: Keep it short and repeat one calm sentence.
Walk away if things heat up. Your child comes first.
Leave the subject for the app.
Tension at handovers? Suggest handing over via school: one of you drops off in the morning, the other picks up after school.
zeg: “I can see this matters to you. Let’s talk about it in the app.”
“I’m going now, the children are waiting.”
liever: “I’m not getting into that now, and you know it.”
A reply to every accusation.
2.onthoud: A conversation that can’t happen now can happen later. Your child doesn’t need to hear it.
2.hulp: you don’t feel safe. Choose a neutral place, hand over via school or with someone else present. If you’re in immediate danger, call 112.
2.kind: An argument at the door comes inside with {kind}. Save it for later. Saying goodbye at school feels like an ordinary day to {kind}: there’s no moment where they see the two of you together.

3.vraag: My child won’t go at the handover, cries or clings to me. What do I do?
3.kort: Children often react to the change itself, not to the other parent. Stay calm, brief and predictable.
doen: Keep the goodbye short and loving.
Tell your child when they’ll see you again.
Try not to let your child see that you’re sad or angry too.
Let them take something familiar with them.
Later, agree a fixed routine with the other parent.
Tension at handovers? Suggest handing over via school: one of you drops off in the morning, the other picks up after school.
zeg: “I love you. I’ll see you on Sunday. I’m always here.”
liever: “You don’t have to go if you don’t want to.”
“I’m going to miss you so much too.” (just as you say goodbye)
3.onthoud: A goodbye that’s hard every time usually gets easier with a fixed routine.
3.hulp: your child stays very sad for a long time, or it gets worse. Talk to your GP or the school.
3.kind: A calm goodbye, without tension between the two of you: that’s what will stay with {kind}. Saying goodbye at school feels like an ordinary day to {kind}: there’s no moment where they see the two of you together.
3.kindKort: Calm between you means calm for {kind}.

4.vraag: The handover went badly and I’m furious. What now?
4.kort: Pause before you do anything. You don’t have to send or decide anything right now.
doen: Breathe out slowly.
Write it down for yourself, not to the other parent.
Wait until tomorrow before you respond.
Then pick one point for a short message.
zeg: “I’d like to come back to this later.”
liever: A long message straight after the handover.
4.onthoud: A message takes a minute to send. The fallout often lasts much longer.
4.kind: Things are allowed to go wrong. What matters to {kind} is how things settle down again afterwards.
4.kindKort: After the storm comes the calm, for {kind} too.

5.vraag: My child comes home with a negative story about the other parent. What do I say?
5.kort: Listen calmly, name what your child is feeling and don’t take sides. You don’t need to confirm or contradict the story.
doen: Listen without interrupting or judging.
Name the feeling: ‘That sounds horrible.’
Ask an open question: ‘What would you like me to know?’
Tell your child it’s okay to love both parents.
If you’re worried, talk calmly to the other parent later, without your child there.
zeg: “That sounds really horrible. I’m glad you told me.”
“I can see that was hard for you.”
liever: “Well, that’s just what he’s like.”
“I could have told you that.”
5.onthoud: Children often say what they’re feeling in that moment. It isn’t always the whole story, and it’s not up to you to decide who’s right.
5.hulp: your child tells you something that worries you, for example about their safety. Talk to a professional or call Veilig Thuis (the Dutch helpline for abuse and child safety): 0800-2000. In immediate danger: 112.
5.kind: It means a lot to {kind} to be allowed to love both parents, without having to take sides.
5.kindKort: Loving you both is allowed. Good for {kind}.

6.vraag: My child says something negative about me, and says the other parent said it. What do I do?
6.kort: Stay calm and acknowledge how your child feels. You don’t need to defend yourself to your child.
doen: Ask what your child heard and how it made them feel.
Say in your own words what you feel: ‘I love you.’
Don’t hit back with something negative.
Talk it over with the other parent later, if you need to.
zeg: “That must have been upsetting to hear. I love you, whatever anyone says.”
liever: “That says more about your mum than about me.”
“What else did she say?”
6.onthoud: What a child passes on often sounds different from how it was meant.
6.kind: Staying calm shows {kind} that nobody has to win between the two of you.
6.kindKort: Nobody has to win. Calm for {kind}.

7.vraag: My child asks whose fault the divorce is.
7.kort: Above all, children need to hear that it isn’t their fault and that both parents love them.
doen: Keep it simple and honest.
Don’t blame either parent.
Say it’s a decision the grown-ups made.
Fit your explanation to your child’s age.
Leave room for questions later on.
zeg: “This is something between Mum and Dad. It’s not your fault. We both love you.”
liever: “Go and ask your dad.”
Details about the relationship.
7.onthoud: You don’t need to have all the answers. ‘I find that hard too’ is an answer as well.
7.kind: When nobody gets the blame, {kind} can simply be a child.
7.kindKort: No blame, so {kind} can just be a child.

8.vraag: My child is sad or angry after a handover. Is that normal?
8.kort: Lots of children need time to settle after a change. Offer calm and predictability.
doen: Keep the first hour quiet.
Don’t ask questions about the other parent.
Stick to your usual routines.
Offer to talk, but don’t push it.
Keep an eye on how long it lasts.
zeg: “I’m so glad you’re back. Let’s take it easy.”
liever: “So, what did you all get up to?” (the moment they walk in)
“Wasn’t it nice there?”
8.onthoud: Children need time. It doesn’t mean something is wrong.
8.hulp: it goes on for a long time or gets worse. Talk to your GP or the school.
8.kind: Sadness after a handover is okay. Your calm helps {kind} settle back in.

9.vraag: I feel angry with the other parent while my child is with me. What should I remember?
9.kort: You’re allowed to be angry. Your child just shouldn’t have to carry it. Find somewhere else for your anger to go.
doen: Find your own outlet: a friend, a journal or Co.
Don’t talk about the other parent when your child is nearby.
Set aside a regular moment for yourself to let it out.
Do something fun with your child.
Is the anger still overwhelming? Talk to your GP or a professional.
zeg: “I’m finding things a bit hard right now, but it’s not because of you. It’ll be okay.”
liever: “Your dad drives me mad.”
Phone calls about the other parent within your child’s earshot.
9.onthoud: Children learn from how you handle difficult feelings, not just from what you say.
9.hulp: you feel you’re losing control. Get help from your GP or your local social support team.
9.kind: Your anger is real. With {kind}, things can simply be nice for a while.
9.kindKort: With {kind}, things can just be nice right now.

10.vraag: How do I stop myself speaking badly about the other parent to my child?
10.kort: One simple rule: say whatever you say about the other parent as if they were standing right there.
doen: Know your triggers, for example after a message or a handover.
Have a neutral sentence ready.
If it slips out anyway, put it right calmly: ‘I shouldn’t have said that.’
Talk to another adult about your frustration.
zeg: “That’s something between Dad and me. You don’t need to worry about it.”
liever: “Your mum broke up our family.”
Sighing or rolling your eyes when the other parent comes up.
10.onthoud: Children often hear more than you think, even when you speak quietly.
10.kind: Every kind word about the other parent is a kind word for {kind} too.
10.kindKort: A kind word about the other parent is kind to {kind} too.

11.vraag: I want to scream. What can I do right now?
11.kort: This feeling will pass. You don’t have to decide anything now.
doen: Breathe out slowly, five times.
Put your phone down and look around you: name five things you can see.
Go for a short walk or move about a bit.
Don’t send anything.
Afterwards, talk to someone you trust.
zeg: “This is a hard moment. It doesn’t need solving right now.”
liever: Anything you fire off straight to the other parent by message or phone.
11.onthoud: Once a message is sent, you can’t take it back, even if you wish you could.
11.kind: Calm yourself first. Then talk, for your own sake and for {kind}.
11.kindKort: Calm for you first, then calm for {kind}.

12.vraag: How do I handle a harsh message from the other parent?
12.kort: You don’t have to reply straight away. Wait, read it again and respond briefly to what actually needs an answer.
doen: Wait a few hours, or until tomorrow.
Look for the facts: what is the other parent really asking?
Reply briefly, with information, kindly and clearly.
Don’t respond to the tone or the accusations.
Ask Co if you’d like some help.
zeg: “Thanks for your message. Saturday doesn’t work for me, but Sunday does. Could you let me know by Wednesday?”
liever: “Why are you always like this?”
A reply that rebuts every single point.
12.onthoud: A reply doesn’t have to rebut everything.
12.kind: A short, calm reply keeps the tension away from {kind}.
12.kindKort: Short and calm: no tension for {kind}.

13.vraag: How do I start a difficult conversation with the other parent?
13.kort: Start small, short and specific. Choose the right moment and the right place, for example the app.
doen: Pick one topic.
Say what you’d like, and ask how the other parent sees it.
Don’t expect it to be sorted straight away.
Give a date by which you need an answer.
zeg: “I’d like to talk about something to do with the holidays. When would be a good time for you to get back to me?”
liever: “We need to talk.”
Three topics in one message.
13.onthoud: You don’t have to solve it all in one go.
13.kind: A good conversation between the two of you quietly supports {kind}.

14.vraag: The other parent doesn’t reply or keeps me waiting. What can I do?
14.kort: Ask clearly and give a date. If you still hear nothing, look for a practical solution.
doen: Ask one clear question.
Give a deadline.
Offer two options.
Only use ‘Quick check-in’ for urgent matters.
Is the silence becoming a pattern? Consider a mediator.
zeg: “Could you let me know by Wednesday? Then I can plan properly.”
liever: “If I don’t hear from you, I’ll decide myself.”
Sending the same message three times.
14.onthoud: Silence isn’t always unwillingness. Sometimes people just need time.
14.kind: Waiting is hard. A calm reminder keeps things light, for {kind} too.
14.kindKort: Staying calm keeps things light for {kind}.

15.vraag: I don’t feel heard. What can I do?
15.kort: Find one sentence that says what you need, without blame.
doen: Write down what you need.
Say ‘I’ instead of ‘you’.
Ask for a short conversation, with a mediator if needed.
Share it with someone you trust, too.
zeg: “I’m noticing I’m finding this hard. It would help me if…”
liever: “You never listen.”
15.onthoud: Being heard often starts with being clear yourself.
15.kind: Wanting to be heard is fair. A calm tone makes all the difference, for {kind} too.
15.kindKort: A calm tone makes all the difference for {kind}.

16.vraag: I can’t cope right now. Where can I turn?
16.kort: Asking for help isn’t failing. You don’t have to do this on your own.
doen: Talk to someone you trust.
Make an appointment with your GP.
Ask your local council about the local social support team or the family support team.
Having thoughts of harming yourself? Call 113 (suicide prevention line), day or night. In immediate danger: 112.
zeg: “I’m having a really hard time and I’d like some help. Could you help me think it through?”
liever: “I’m fine.” (when you’re not)
16.onthoud: A calm parent helps a child more than a perfect parent.
16.hulp: you’re having thoughts of harming yourself. Call 113 or your GP. In immediate danger: 112.
16.kind: Looking after yourself is also looking after {kind}.
16.kindKort: Caring for you is caring for {kind}.

17.vraag: The other parent is late or doesn’t turn up. What do I do?
17.kort: Look after your child first. The conversation about arrangements can come later, calmly and in the app.
doen: Wait a set time, say fifteen minutes, then send one short message.
Explain to your child what’s happening, without judging.
Then do something ordinary together.
Make a note of the date, without building a case.
Does it keep happening? Suggest a fixed arrangement, such as a text if they’re running late.
zeg: To your child: “Mum’s running a bit late. We’ll wait a little longer, and then we’ll read a book.” To the other parent: “We’ll wait until 17:15. Could you let me know what time you’ll be here?”
liever: “See? He’s never on time.”
“Your dad thinks other things are more important.”
17.onthoud: Your child learns from how you deal with disappointment.
17.hulp: it happens a lot and you can’t sort it out together. A mediator can help you make clear arrangements.
17.kind: Waiting is no fun. A calm tone makes the wait easier for {kind}.
17.kindKort: Your calm makes the wait easier for {kind}.

18.vraag: The other parent’s new partner is at the handover. How do I handle it?
18.kort: That can hurt. It helps your child if you stay polite and brief, whatever you feel about it.
doen: Say a short, friendly hello.
Only discuss things with the other parent.
Decide beforehand what you will and won’t discuss with the partner there.
Agree with the other parent how you’d both like this to go, for example without the partner at first.
Check what your parenting plan says about a new partner.
zeg: “Hi.”
“Could we do the handovers just the two of us for a while? That would be easier for me right now.”
liever: Comments about the partner in front of your child.
18.onthoud: How you react now helps decide how free your child feels at the other home.
18.kind: A friendly nod to the new partner makes things easier for {kind}.
18.kindKort: A nod is enough. Good for {kind}.

19.vraag: Something important has been forgotten, like medicine or school things. What now?
19.kort: That happens with two homes. Sort it out practically, and use a fixed list to prevent it next time.
doen: First check what your child needs today.
Send one practical message, without blame.
Offer to collect or drop it off if you can.
Add it to the fixed list in the Handover packing list.
For medicine: agree to keep a supply in both homes.
zeg: “Noah’s inhaler is still at yours. Could I pick it up at 18:00?”
liever: “You always forget everything.”
19.onthoud: A list prevents more arguments than a telling-off.
19.hulp: your child is missing medicine they need. Call your GP or pharmacy for advice.
19.kind: A forgotten item can be sorted. Without blame, it stays an ordinary day for {kind}.
19.kindKort: Without blame, it stays an ordinary day for {kind}.

20.vraag: My child seems to feel guilty about having a good time at the other parent’s. What do I do?
20.kort: Your child doesn’t want to hurt you. Show them clearly that they’re allowed to enjoy both homes.
doen: Ask with genuine interest about something nice at the other home.
Let your child see it makes you happy when they’ve had a good time.
Don’t let your child carry how much you missed them.
Don’t tell them how quiet the house was without them.
zeg: “How lovely that you went to the beach. Tell me all about it.”
“You’re allowed to have a good time everywhere.”
liever: “I was so lonely this weekend.”
“It’s nice here too, isn’t it?”
20.onthoud: A child who doesn’t have to choose has more room to just be a child.
20.kind: Enjoying both homes is the best thing there is for {kind}.
20.kindKort: Happiness in two homes is golden for {kind}.

21.vraag: My child doesn’t want to go to the other parent. What do I do?
21.kort: Take the feeling seriously, but the arrangement stays. First find out what’s behind it.
doen: Calmly ask what your child is finding hard.
Say you understand, and that the arrangement still stands.
Talk it through with the other parent, without your child there.
Look together at what might help, like a set ritual or a shorter first day.
Don’t turn the conversation with your child into a choice.
zeg: “I can hear this feels hard. Dad’s really looking forward to seeing you. What would make it easier?”
liever: “You don’t have to go if you don’t want to.”
“I get it, it’s no fun at his place either.”
21.onthoud: The parenting plan still applies, even when things are hard for a while.
21.hulp: it goes on for a long time, your child seems frightened, or tells you something that worries you. Talk to your GP, a child coach or Veilig Thuis: 0800-2000.
21.kind: The calmer things are between the two of you, the easier the step to the other home is for {kind}.
21.kindKort: Calm between you makes the step smaller for {kind}.

22.vraag: My child passes messages between us, or asks me to keep a secret.
22.kort: Messages between parents aren’t a child’s job. Gently take your child out of it and sort it out with the other parent yourself.
doen: Thank your child and say you’ll take it from here.
Send the other parent a message yourself.
Never ask your child to pass something on or keep something quiet.
If it’s a secret: listen, and explain that sometimes grown-ups need to know things so they can take good care of them.
zeg: “Thanks for telling me. I’ll sort this out with Mum myself, you don’t need to.”
liever: “Tell your dad that…”
“Mum doesn’t need to know about this.”
22.onthoud: A child who doesn’t have to carry messages can simply be at home in both places.
22.kind: No messages and no secrets: that keeps things light for {kind}.
22.kindKort: Not being the messenger: lighter for {kind}.

23.vraag: My child wants to choose where to live, or wants a different schedule.
23.kort: An older child can have a say. You make the decision together as parents, with your child’s best interests first.
doen: Listen to the reason without reacting straight away.
Say you take it seriously and will talk it over with the other parent.
Discuss it together as parents first.
Check what your parenting plan says about reviews and your child’s wishes.
Can’t agree? Ask a mediator or a children’s advocate.
zeg: “I’m glad you told me. Dad and I will talk about it and come back to you.”
liever: “Well, just come and live with me then.”
“Why don’t you want to go to Mum’s any more?”
23.onthoud: Having a say is not the same as having to choose.
23.kind: Choosing between parents is too heavy. Deciding together lifts that weight off {kind}.
23.kindKort: Deciding together lifts the weight off {kind}.

24.vraag: My child plays us off against each other.
24.kort: That’s very common for children with two homes. It works less well once you check with each other.
doen: Don’t react straight away to ‘But Dad lets me!’
Calmly check with the other parent.
Agree a few house rules that apply in both homes.
Accept that the other home can have different rules.
zeg: To your child: “Things might be different at Dad’s. Here, this is how we do it.” To the other parent: “Emma says she can stay up until ten at yours. Is that right? Just so I know.”
liever: “Dad lets you? Typical.”
24.onthoud: Two homes with different rules is fine. Two parents who don’t check with each other is not.
24.kind: When you’re on the same page, there’s nothing to play off. That gives {kind} something steady to hold on to.
24.kindKort: Being on the same page steadies {kind}.

25.vraag: I keep getting messages in the evening or at the weekend. Do I have to reply?
25.kort: No. You decide when you reply, unless it’s genuinely urgent.
doen: Turn on quiet hours in Quiet mode.
Pick one set time a day to read messages.
Let them know when you’ll reply, without explaining why.
Agree what counts as urgent, for example illness or pick-ups.
zeg: “I read messages every day around 18:00. If it’s urgent, please use ‘Quick check-in’.”
liever: “Can you just leave me alone for once?”
25.onthoud: A calm moment to reply makes for a calmer reply.
25.kind: Boundaries around messages give you breathing space, and so they give {kind} space too.
25.kindKort: Your calm is calm for {kind} too.

26.vraag: The other parent has a new partner and it hurts.
26.kort: That’s an understandable feeling. It’s yours, and it doesn’t have to pass through your child.
doen: Give yourself time. Hurt, jealousy or sadness are all allowed.
Talk about it with another adult, not with your child.
Don’t quiz your child about the new partner.
Let your child know it’s fine to like the partner.
Check what you agreed about new relationships in your parenting plan.
zeg: To your child: “I’m glad you have a nice time there.”
liever: “So what’s she like?”
“You don’t have to like her, you know.”
26.onthoud: Your child can love an extra adult without loving you any less.
26.hulp: the feeling is with you every day. Your GP can refer you to a mental health practitioner.
26.kind: Your sadness is allowed. How the two of you treat each other is still what matters most to {kind}.
26.kindKort: How you treat each other matters most to {kind}.

27.vraag: I asked for a change and the other parent said no. What now?
27.kort: Then the arrangement in your parenting plan still applies. The other parent is allowed to say no, even without a reason.
doen: Read the reply and wait a little before answering.
See whether a different proposal might work.
If it doesn’t work out, accept it. The usual arrangement applies.
Does this keep going wrong? Your plan often names a mediator you can call on.
zeg: “Fair enough, we’ll keep it as it is.”
“Would it work if I bring them back on Sunday at 12:00?”
liever: “Well, I’m never doing anything for you again.”
27.onthoud: An arrangement stands until you make a new one together.
27.hulp: you often can’t agree. A mediator can help. Going to court is the last step.
27.kind: A no isn’t a fight. Calmly looking for another way gives {kind} confidence.
27.kindKort: A no doesn’t have to be a fight, for {kind}’s sake.

28.vraag: We keep arguing about costs. How can I prevent that?
28.kort: Agree in advance what you share and what you don’t. Arguments usually start afterwards.
doen: Suggest a budget before any big expense.
Attach the receipt to the expense.
For each expense, choose which account it was paid from.
Agree a limit, for example: anything over € 50, check first.
Keep money and care arrangements separate.
zeg: “Noah needs new football boots, about € 60. Shall we split them?”
liever: “You never pay for anything.”
Talking about money at the handover.
28.onthoud: Agreeing beforehand costs less than arguing afterwards.
28.kind: Money is something between adults. That way it stays out of sight for {kind}.
28.kindKort: Money stays out of sight for {kind}.

29.vraag: Child maintenance isn’t being paid, or not on time.
29.kort: Keep it businesslike. Point to the arrangement and the date, without turning it into a fight.
doen: Send one short, factual message.
Keep a note of dates and amounts for yourself.
Ask whether something’s going on, and whether a different payment date would help.
Never involve your child.
Still not paid? A legal adviser or the LBIO (the Dutch child maintenance collection agency) can explain your options.
zeg: “I haven’t received the payment for November yet. Could you transfer it this week?”
liever: “Then Emma can’t go to swimming lessons, thanks to you.”
29.onthoud: Money is a matter between adults.
29.hulp: payments still don’t arrive. Ask a legal adviser or the LBIO for information. This is not legal advice.
29.kind: Deal with money matters out of sight. That keeps things carefree for {kind}.
29.kindKort: Money matters out of sight of {kind}.

30.vraag: Something big needs deciding, like school, treatment or a trip abroad.
30.kort: With joint parental responsibility, you decide this together. Give the other parent all the information in good time.
doen: Put it in the app as ‘Needs discussion’, with the facts and a date.
Share information from the school or care provider with the other parent.
Ask what the other parent needs in order to decide.
Write down the decision once you agree.
For a trip abroad: ask for written consent in good time.
zeg: “The orthodontist recommends a brace. I’ve attached the advice. Could we decide by Friday?”
liever: “I’ve already sorted it.”
30.onthoud: Keeping each other informed in good time stops anyone feeling left out.
30.hulp: you can’t agree. A mediator can help. If you’re unsure about the legal side, ask a legal adviser.
30.kind: Choosing a school or care together lets {kind} feel that you’re both there for them.
30.kindKort: Choosing together gives {kind} something to hold on to.

31.vraag: The house is so quiet when the children are with the other parent.
31.kort: Missing them is normal, especially at first. This time can be yours too.
doen: Plan something for the first evening, even something small.
Create a little ritual, like a walk or calling someone.
Leave your child’s room just as it is.
Call or message your child as agreed, not extra times to reassure yourself.
Spend time with people who give you energy.
zeg: To your child: “Have a lovely few days. See you on Tuesday.”
liever: “I’m going to miss you so much, it’s so empty here without you.”
31.onthoud: Your child finds it easier to go when they know you’ll be okay.
31.hulp: missing them leaves you feeling low for a long time. Talk to your GP.
31.kind: The quiet is hard. Look after yourself, and there’ll be plenty of room for {kind} again soon.
31.kindKort: Look after yourself, then there’s room for {kind}.

32.vraag: The first holidays or celebrations without my child.
32.kort: The first year is often the hardest. Plan ahead how you’ll spend these days for yourself.
doen: Check the calendar well ahead to see when your child is with the other parent.
Plan something with people who do you good.
Create your own moment with your child, before or after the day itself.
Call at the agreed time and keep it short and warm.
Be gentle with yourself if it’s hard.
zeg: “We’re celebrating Christmas on 27 December, just the two of us. I’m really looking forward to it.”
liever: “I’ll be all on my own at Christmas.”
32.onthoud: A celebration on a different day is just as real to a child.
32.kind: A happy holiday at the other parent’s is a gift for {kind}, even if it hurts you.
32.kindKort: A happy day at the other home is a gift for {kind}.

33.vraag: I feel guilty towards my child because of the divorce.
33.kort: Feeling guilty shows how much your child means to you. What your child needs most is a parent who is there for them now.
doen: Stick to your usual rules and routines, even when you feel guilty.
Don’t make up for it with presents or fewer boundaries.
Tell your child it’s okay to show what they feel.
Talk about your own guilt with another adult.
zeg: “It’s a big change. You can ask me anything.”
liever: “I’m sorry I ruined your life.”
33.onthoud: A child gets more from a parent who is there than from one who tries to make everything up to them.
33.kind: It doesn’t have to be perfect. Every calm moment counts for {kind}.

34.vraag: I have a new partner. When and how do I tell my child?
34.kort: Take your time, and tell the other parent first. That way your child doesn’t hear it second-hand.
doen: Wait until the relationship is stable.
Tell the other parent first, as many parenting plans agree.
Agree together when and how your child will hear about it.
Keep the first meeting short and relaxed, somewhere neutral.
Give your child time and room to have their own feelings about it.
zeg: To the other parent: “I’d like to tell you something before the children hear it.” To your child: “I’ve met someone I really like. You’ll always be the most important person to me.”
liever: “This is your new mum.”
“You don’t need to tell Dad.”
34.onthoud: Words like Mum and Dad stay with the parents, unless you agree something else together.
34.kind: Telling them calmly and in good time, and letting the other parent know first, saves {kind} a lot of unrest.
34.kindKort: Tell the other parent first: calm for {kind}.

35.vraag: My child is going on holiday with the other parent. How do I arrange it well?
35.kort: Agree the practical things beforehand. Then your child can go without any worries.
doen: Add the holiday to the calendar according to your arrangement.
Ask for the address and an emergency phone number.
Send passport, health insurance card and medicine along via the Handover packing list.
For a trip abroad, sort out consent in good time.
Agree when you’ll phone or video call.
zeg: “Have a lovely holiday. Shall we video call on Sunday evening?”
liever: “Call me if you miss me and I’ll come and get you.”
35.onthoud: Your child enjoys it more when they know you’re happy for them to go.
35.kind: A good start to the holiday, without tension at the goodbye, is lovely for {kind}.
35.kindKort: A calm departure is lovely for {kind}.

36.vraag: My child’s birthday. How do we celebrate?
36.kort: First check what you’ve agreed. Above all, your child should feel the day is a celebration.
doen: Check your parenting plan to see whether you celebrate together or separately.
Coordinate presents, so your child doesn’t get the same thing twice.
Is the other parent celebrating on the day? Plan your own party the day before or after.
Don’t turn the day into a contest over who throws the best party.
zeg: To the other parent: “I’d like to give Emma a bike. What did you have in mind?”
liever: “You’ll get a proper party at mine.”
36.onthoud: For a child, two parties often just means twice the fun.
36.kind: A birthday without tension between the two of you is the best present for {kind}.
36.kindKort: No tension: the best present for {kind}.

37.vraag: Mother’s Day, Father’s Day or the other parent’s birthday is coming up.
37.kort: Help your child make or buy something for the other parent. It gives your child room to love you both.
doen: Check the calendar a week ahead.
Help with a craft or a card, even if it’s hard for you.
See whether your plan says your child spends that day with the parent being celebrated.
Let your child choose what to give.
zeg: “It’s Father’s Day on Sunday. Shall we make something for Dad together?”
liever: “He can sort that out himself.”
37.onthoud: What you do for the other parent now, you’re really doing for your child.
37.kind: Helping with a card or present for the other parent leaves {kind} free to love you both.
37.kindKort: Being free to love you both is lovely for {kind}.

38.vraag: The other parent or I am moving house.
38.kort: A move affects your arrangements. Talk it through beforehand, even if the parenting plan allows it.
doen: Discuss the plan with the other parent in good time.
Look at what changes for travel time, school and handovers.
Adjust the arrangements together and put them in writing.
Involve your child in practical choices, like how to decorate their room.
Is a parent planning to move far away? Then talking it through together is even more important. If in doubt, ask a legal adviser.
zeg: “I’d like to tell you about a possible move. Could we look at what it would mean for the handovers?”
liever: “I’ve already signed, it’s all sorted.”
38.onthoud: A move shouldn’t get in the way of the agreed contact.
38.hulp: you can’t agree. A mediator can help. Going to court is the last step.
38.kind: Arranging a move well together gives {kind} the feeling that both homes are here to stay.

39.vraag: We’re both going to a parents’ evening or a school performance.
39.kort: Your child loves it when you’re both there. A polite hello is enough.
doen: For a meeting at school, agree beforehand who will ask what.
Greet each other briefly and kindly.
Sit wherever feels comfortable for you.
Afterwards, discuss only what’s needed, in the app.
zeg: “Hi. Shall I ask about maths and you ask about the test?”
liever: Discussing your own issues in front of the teacher.
39.onthoud: What matters most to your child is that you’re both there.
39.kind: A quick nod or hello at parents’ evening, so all the attention can go to {kind}.
39.kindKort: A hello is enough. All eyes on {kind}.

40.vraag: I’m worried about how things are going at the other parent’s.
40.kort: Take your worry seriously and look at the facts. If there’s immediate danger, act straight away. Otherwise, talk to the other parent or a professional first.
doen: Write down what you see or hear, with the date, without filling in the gaps.
Don’t quiz your child or ask them to check on anything for you.
Raise a worry calmly with the other parent, if it’s safe to do so.
Ask your GP, the school or Veilig Thuis for advice.
zeg: “I’m worried about Noah. Could we look together at what’s going on?”
liever: To your child: “Keep an eye on what Dad’s doing.”
40.onthoud: Sharing a worry is not the same as making an accusation.
40.hulp: you’re worried about your child’s safety. Call Veilig Thuis: 0800-2000, also for advice. In immediate danger: 112.
40.kind: Take your worries seriously and act calmly. That helps {kind} most.
