1.vraag: My child can't sleep at night because they miss the other parent.
1.kort: Missing someone is actually a lovely thing: it shows your child loves you both. In the evening, when it gets quiet and dark, the feeling often comes up. You don't have to fix it. Simply being there already helps a great deal.
doen: Sit or lie down next to your child and name the feeling, without talking it away.
Keep the bedtime routine exactly the same: reading aloud, a familiar song, the light on or off.
Show on the calendar when your child will see the other parent again. Counting in nights helps young children.
Agree a regular call time with the other parent, well before bedtime.
Let your child keep something of the other parent close: a photo, a cuddly toy or a jumper.

zeg.samen: You miss Dad/Mum. That's completely fine. You'll see him/her again on Saturday. Shall I stay with you a little longer?
zeg.jong: You miss Dad/Mum. That's OK. Two more sleeps and you'll see him/her again. I'll stay with you until you fall asleep.
zeg.midden: I can see you miss Dad/Mum. That's a good thing, because it means you love each other very much. Shall we give him/her a call together tomorrow?
zeg.oud: It's OK to miss him/her. Would you like to send a message before you go to sleep? That's absolutely fine with me.

reageren.kind: "Why can't Dad/Mum sleep here?"
reageren.jij: "Dad/Mum has a home of his/her own now. You sleep there too, and you have a bed there as well. Now you have two places where someone is waiting for you."

reageren.kind: "I can't sleep without Dad/Mum."
reageren.jij: "That feels really hard right now. I'm staying with you. Shall we think together about what you'd like to tell him/her tomorrow?"

liever: "But you're with me now, aren't you?"
"Don't be so sad, it's only a few days."
1.idee: Make a "missing box" together: a box next to the bed with a photo, a drawing for the other parent and the calendar. When the missing comes, your child reaches for the box.
1.kind: If {kind} can miss Dad/Mum without you getting sad, {kind} feels safe with both of you.
1.voorJou: It can hurt that your child misses the other parent while you're right there. That's human. Simply being there is you doing it well.
1.hulp: Has your child been sleeping badly for weeks on end, or are they very tired or anxious during the day? Talk to your GP or health visitor.

2.vraag: My child cries and says: I want to go to Dad/Mum.
2.kort: Your child isn't saying they don't want to be with you. They're saying they miss the other parent. Both can be true at once. Comfort first; talking comes later.
doen: Stay calm and don't take it personally, however hard that is.
Comfort first: an arm around your child says more than words.
Offer something from the other parent: a photo, a voice message, a cuddly toy.
Help your child do something with the feeling, such as making a drawing for the other parent.

zeg.samen: You want to go to Dad/Mum. I understand. Shall we look at a photo of him/her together?
zeg.jong: You want Dad/Mum. Come here to me. Let's have a cuddle first, then we'll look at the calendar.
zeg.midden: You're really missing Dad/Mum right now. That's OK. Would you like to make a drawing to take with you on Saturday?
zeg.oud: I can tell you're missing him/her right now. Would you like to call? That's absolutely fine.

reageren.kind: "It's much more fun at Dad's/Mum's."
reageren.jij: "I'm glad you have fun there. What do you like so much about it? Maybe we can think of something here too."

reageren.kind: "I want to go to Dad/Mum NOW."
reageren.jij: "I hear you. It can't be now, but it can on Saturday. What would help you right now?"

liever: "But it's nice here with me too, isn't it?"
"Well, off you go to him/her then."
2.idee: Record a voice message for the other parent together: what your child did today. It gives a sense of connection without needing a phone call.
2.kind: {kind} can miss the other parent without being afraid that it will make you sad.
2.voorJou: It isn't personal, even if it feels that way. Your child is showing you their sadness precisely because they feel safe with you.

3.vraag: My child wants to call the other parent every evening.
3.kort: Contact with the other parent gives your child something to hold on to. A fixed arrangement works better than deciding afresh every evening: that way everyone knows where they stand.
doen: Agree a fixed time and a fixed length of call with the other parent.
Choose a time well before bed, so your child can settle afterwards.
Give your child space during the call; don't listen in once they're old enough.
A message, photo or voice note in between is fine too, if you both agree.

zeg.samen: At seven o'clock you'll call Dad/Mum. Then you can tell him/her everything.
zeg.jong: After tea we'll call Dad/Mum. What would you like to show him/her?
zeg.midden: On Wednesday and Sunday you call Dad/Mum. That way you really have time for him/her.
zeg.oud: You can always send Dad/Mum a message. We do calls at seven, so it's not too late.

reageren.kind: "Can I call one more time?"
reageren.jij: "You'd really like to hear him/her again, wouldn't you? You'll call again tomorrow. Shall we send a goodnight message now?"

reageren.kind: "Dad/Mum isn't answering."
reageren.jij: "What a shame. Maybe he/she is busy for a moment. Let's send a message, then he/she can call you back when possible."

liever: "Not this again?"
"You're with me now, so no calling."
3.idee: Make a call calendar together with the fixed call times on it. Your child can put a sticker on it after each call.
3.kind: Knowing when {kind} will hear from the other parent again makes the missing smaller.
3.voorJou: It might feel as if the other parent is taking up your time too. Remember: every call makes your child calmer, and that helps you as well.

4.vraag: After the handover my child is restless or upset on the first evening.
4.kort: Every handover is a transition for a child: saying goodbye, getting used to different sounds, different rules. Restlessness on the first evening is completely normal. It's not a sign that things went badly at the other parent's.
doen: Plan very little for the first evening: no visitors, no busy activities.
Start with a regular welcome ritual, for example having a drink together on the sofa.
Don't ask straight away how it was; give your child time to land first.
Put your child's things straight back in their usual place.

zeg.samen: Lovely to have you back. Let's take it easy tonight.
zeg.jong: Welcome home. Shall we sit on the sofa together first?
zeg.midden: Good to have you here. You don't have to tell me anything. If you want to, I'm here.
zeg.oud: Welcome back. Feel free to take some time for yourself, I'm downstairs.

reageren.kind: Your child is quiet or grumpy.
reageren.jij: "It takes a bit of getting used to, being back here, doesn't it? I understand. We won't do anything difficult tonight."

reageren.kind: "At Dad's/Mum's I'm allowed to stay up later."
reageren.jij: "Things are different there, and here we do it like this. Tonight we'll go to bed on time, so you're well rested tomorrow."

liever: "What's the matter with you now?"
"So, how was it there? What did you do?" (the moment they walk in)
4.idee: Come up with a regular welcome ritual together: pancakes on Friday, a mug of hot chocolate, a walk with the dog. It makes the transition feel familiar.
4.kind: A calm first evening helps {kind} to settle back into your home.
4.voorJou: You don't have to be all fun straight away. Giving them some calm is enough.

5.vraag: My child wants to have something from the other parent with them.
5.kort: A jumper that smells of Dad/Mum, a cuddly toy from the other home: things like this are a bridge between two homes. They help your child feel safe.
doen: Allow it, even if the item belongs to the other parent.
Agree with the other parent that items like these can travel freely.
Give the item a fixed place, so it doesn't get lost.

zeg.samen: Of course you can bring that. Then Dad/Mum is close by.
zeg.jong: Your cuddly toy from Dad/Mum can sleep here. Nice, isn't it?
zeg.midden: I like that you're wearing his/her jumper. It feels like he/she is close by.
zeg.oud: Bring whatever you like. They're your things.

reageren.kind: "Can I have the photo of Dad/Mum next to my bed?"
reageren.jij: "Yes, of course. Shall we find a nice spot for it together?"

liever: "We don't need his/her stuff here."
5.idee: Let your child take something of yours to the other home too, such as a photo or a letter to open when they miss you.
5.kind: Something from the other parent gives {kind} the feeling that both homes belong together.
5.voorJou: It can sting a little to see the other parent's things in your home. It says nothing about you, and everything about how your child looks for something to hold on to.

6.vraag: My baby or toddler misses the other parent but can't say so.
6.kort: Young children show they miss someone rather than saying it: crying more, sleeping worse, being extra clingy. Predictability and the same rituals in both homes help most.
doen: Keep routines and rituals in both homes as similar as possible: meals, sleep, the bedtime song.
Use the same comfort blanket or sleeping bag, and let it travel with them.
Show photos of the other parent and call him or her by name.
Agree short, frequent moments with the other parent; for young children, more often and shorter works better.

zeg.samen: Look, there's Dad/Mum in the photo. You'll see him/her again tomorrow.
zeg.jong: You're looking for Dad/Mum, aren't you? Dad/Mum is coming tomorrow. Mum/Dad is here.
zeg.midden: You're looking for Dad/Mum, aren't you? Dad/Mum is coming tomorrow. Mum/Dad is here.
zeg.oud: You're looking for Dad/Mum, aren't you? Dad/Mum is coming tomorrow. Mum/Dad is here.

reageren.kind: Your child cries at the door after the handover.
reageren.jij: Pick your child up, calmly say "I'm here" and do something familiar together, like reading a book.

liever: Quickly distracting them without acknowledging the sadness.
6.idee: Make a photo book with both homes and both parents. Leafing through it together helps young children understand they have two homes.
6.kind: For a very young child, predictability means safety: {kind} then knows what's coming.
6.voorJou: A young child who cries more says nothing about how well you care for him or her. It shows that a lot is changing.
6.hulp: Is your baby or toddler crying much more than usual, eating or drinking poorly, or are you worried? Go to your health visitor or GP.

7.vraag: My child doesn't dare to say they had a nice time at the other parent's.
7.kort: Children don't want to hurt their parents. That's why they sometimes keep happy stories to themselves. Once your child notices they're allowed to be happy about the other parent, they no longer need to hide anything.
doen: Ask openly how it was, and respond warmly to happy stories.
Don't let it show if you find it hard; talk about that later with another adult.
Say on your own initiative that you hope they had a nice time.
Ask about the details: it shows you're genuinely interested.

zeg.samen: Did you have a nice time at Dad's/Mum's? Tell me about it, I'd love to hear.
zeg.jong: What did you do at Dad's/Mum's? Was it fun?
zeg.midden: I like it when you have a good time at Dad's/Mum's. What did you get up to?
zeg.oud: You can just tell me if it was nice. That makes me happy.

reageren.kind: "It was quite nice…" (hesitantly)
reageren.jij: "How lovely! What was the best bit? I'm glad you had a good time."

reageren.kind: "We went to the zoo with Dad/Mum."
reageren.jij: "How fun! Which animal did you like best?"

liever: "Well, nice for you."
"And were you allowed to do all that there?"
7.idee: At dinner, ask about "the best thing this week", in both homes. That way talking about the other parent becomes something ordinary.
7.kind: If {kind} can talk happily about the other parent, {kind} doesn't have to be a different child in each home.
7.voorJou: Being happy for your child about time spent with the other parent is a big thing. It's one of the most precious things you can give.

8.vraag: My child says they'd rather live with me, or takes sides.
8.kort: A child who picks a side often feels under pressure or wants to protect someone. You help most by showing them they don't have to choose, even if they choose you.
doen: Listen for what's behind it: is something difficult at the other parent's, or does your child want to comfort you?
Say clearly that your child is allowed to love you both.
Don't speak badly of the other parent, even if your child does.
Discuss it calmly with the other parent, without using your child as a messenger.

zeg.samen: You don't have to choose. Mum and Dad both love you, and you're allowed to love us both.
zeg.jong: You don't have to choose. You have a home with me and a home with Dad/Mum.
zeg.midden: I'm glad you like being with me. You can love Dad/Mum too, and that's absolutely fine with me.
zeg.oud: I hear you. What makes it hard at Dad's/Mum's? Then we can look together at what's possible.

reageren.kind: "Dad/Mum is stupid, you're much nicer."
reageren.jij: "I can tell you're angry with Dad/Mum. What happened? You're allowed to be angry, and you're also allowed to love him/her."

reageren.kind: "I don't want to go to Dad/Mum any more."
reageren.jij: "It sounds like something is difficult. Will you tell me? Then I'll work out with Dad/Mum how to make it better."

liever: "I get it, it's not much fun with him/her."
"Well, you'll have to tell Dad/Mum that yourself."
8.idee: Say regularly, even when nothing has happened: "You're allowed to love us both." Children only really take it in when they hear it often.
8.kind: {kind} isn't caught in the middle when you both make it clear: you're allowed to love us both.
8.voorJou: It can feel good when your child chooses you. Yet you give your child the most by not letting them make that choice.
8.hulp: Has your child not wanted to go to the other parent for a long time, or are they frightened? Talk to your GP, a youth care worker or a mediator.

9.vraag: My child wants to look after me or keeps an eye on how I'm feeling.
9.kort: Children sense unerringly when a parent is struggling. They don't need to carry that worry. Show that adults are looking after you, so your child can be a child again.
doen: Say that you're sad, and that you're taking care of that yourself.
Look for support from adults: friends, family or a professional.
Let your child be a child: playing, school, friends.
Thank your child for caring, and kindly hand the responsibility back.

zeg.samen: Sometimes I'm sad, but I take care of that myself. You don't need to look after me.
zeg.jong: Mum/Dad is sad sometimes. It'll pass. You go and play.
zeg.midden: It's sweet that you're thinking of me. I have people who help me. You don't have to look after me.
zeg.oud: I can see you're keeping an eye on me. Thank you. But I'll sort it out myself, with people around me. You just do your own thing.

reageren.kind: "I'll stay home tonight, otherwise you'll be on your own."
reageren.jij: "That's so kind of you to think of me. You go and see your friend. I've got a nice evening planned."

reageren.kind: "Are you sad, Mum/Dad?"
reageren.jij: "Yes, sometimes. That's OK, and it passes. I have people to talk to."

liever: "You're the man/woman of the house now."
"Thank goodness I've still got you."
9.idee: Deliberately plan something nice for yourself while your child is with the other parent, and tell them about it. That way your child sees that you're coping.
9.kind: {kind} can relax once {kind} knows the grown-ups are taking care of themselves.
9.voorJou: You don't always have to be strong. Showing sadness is fine; letting your child look after you is not. Look for support from adults.
9.hulp: Do you notice your child putting on a brave face or constantly worrying? Talk to your GP or the school. Getting support yourself helps your child too.

10.vraag: My child passes on messages from the other parent.
10.kort: "Dad says you were late." Children pick up a lot and pass it on, sometimes because they've been asked to. A child used as a messenger is caught in the middle. Gently take them out of it.
doen: Don't respond to the content of the message while your child is there.
Thank your child and say you'll sort this out with the other parent yourself.
Agree with the other parent that you'll inform each other directly, for example through the app.
Never give your child messages to pass on yourself either.

zeg.samen: Thank you. Dad and I will sort this out ourselves. You don't need to pass anything on.
zeg.jong: Thank you. I'll sort that out with Dad/Mum.
zeg.midden: Thanks for telling me. I'll sort this out with Dad/Mum myself, you don't need to pass anything on.
zeg.oud: I'm glad you told me. But you don't have to stand between us. I'll discuss it myself.

reageren.kind: "Dad/Mum says you spend too much money."
reageren.jij: "That's something between Dad/Mum and me. You don't need to worry about it."

reageren.kind: "Dad/Mum wants to know if I can stay longer on Saturday."
reageren.jij: "Thanks for telling me. I'll send Dad/Mum a message myself."

liever: "Tell your father/mother that…"
"What else did he/she say?"
10.idee: Agree with the other parent: everything about planning and money goes through the app, never through the children.
10.kind: {kind} can just be a child when {kind} doesn't have to pass anything on.
10.voorJou: It's tempting to react to what your child passes on. Biting your tongue and sorting it out with the other parent yourself protects your child.

11.vraag: My child tells each of us something different.
11.kort: Children sometimes say what a parent wants to hear, so as not to disappoint anyone. It isn't lying, it's loyalty. It helps if you as parents stay well aligned.
doen: Don't accuse your child of lying.
Calmly check with the other parent what's going on, without your child there.
Show your child that being honest is safe: you won't get angry or sad.

zeg.samen: You can tell both of us anything. We won't be cross.
zeg.jong: You can always say what you really think.
zeg.midden: You don't have to say what I want to hear. I just want to know how it is for you.
zeg.oud: I can tell you sometimes feel caught between us. You're allowed to be honest, even if it's something I don't like hearing.

reageren.kind: "I don't like it at all at Dad's/Mum's." (and says the opposite there)
reageren.jij: "What do you find difficult? Go on, you can say anything." Then discuss it calmly with the other parent.

liever: "You're lying."
"You always tell your father/mother something different too."
11.idee: Let your child see that you as parents are in touch about everyday things. Then they don't have to act as a bridge between you.
11.kind: Once {kind} notices that honesty doesn't hurt anyone, {kind} dares to say what they really feel again.
11.voorJou: It's confusing when your child says contradictory things. It says something about the pressure they feel, not about you.

12.vraag: My child is angry with me, or with the other parent.
12.kort: Anger is often sadness in disguise. A child who is angry with a parent doesn't love them any less. They feel safe enough to show it.
doen: Stay calm and don't take the anger personally.
Name the feeling, and set limits on the behaviour.
Later, when things are calm, ask what's going on.
Offer an outlet: running, stamping, punching a pillow, drawing.

zeg.samen: You're angry. That's allowed. Hitting or kicking isn't. Shall we talk together in a little while?
zeg.jong: You're really angry. Come on, let's stamp it away together.
zeg.midden: I understand you're angry. Everything is different. Do you want to tell me what you think is the worst part?
zeg.oud: You're allowed to be angry, even with me. I'm not going anywhere. If you want to talk, I'm here.

reageren.kind: "I hate you! You ruined everything."
reageren.jij: "You're very angry and sad. I understand. I love you, even now." Later: "Do you want to tell me what you find hardest?"

reageren.kind: "It's all Dad's/Mum's fault."
reageren.jij: "You're angry with Dad/Mum. That's allowed. It's something between us grown-ups. You can still love him/her."

liever: "Don't you talk to me like that." (in the heat of the moment)
"You're just like your father/mother."
12.idee: Make an anger thermometer together: from green (calm) to purple (very angry). Your child points to how they feel, without needing words.
12.kind: If {kind} can be angry without losing anyone, the sadness underneath can come out too.
12.voorJou: Angry words from your child can hit hard. Your child picks you because they know you'll stay. That says something lovely about your bond.

13.vraag: My child doesn't talk about it and withdraws.
13.kort: Children rarely bring it up themselves. Being quiet doesn't mean things are fine. Show that you're there, without forcing it.
doen: Ask now and then how things are going, even when nothing seems wrong.
Talk side by side rather than face to face: in the car, on a walk or while cooking.
Use a book or film about two homes to open the conversation.
Show that you notice: a wink, sitting down next to your child for a moment.

zeg.samen: You can always ask me anything, including about Mum and Dad.
zeg.jong: Shall we make a drawing of your two homes?
zeg.midden: You don't have to say anything. But if you want to talk, I'm here.
zeg.oud: I'm not asking to force you. I just want to know how you're doing.

reageren.kind: "It's fine." or "I don't know."
reageren.jij: "OK. If you want to talk later, that's always fine. Even in the middle of the night."

liever: "There's nothing wrong, is there?"
"Why do you never say anything?"
13.idee: Leave out a notebook in which your child can write or draw something, and you write back. For some children that's easier than talking.
13.kind: Even if {kind} says nothing, {kind} notices that you see it. That already means a lot.
13.voorJou: It's hard when your child shuts down. Keep the door open; children often come to you at an unexpected moment.
13.hulp: Has your child been withdrawn for weeks, or no longer wants to go to school or see friends? Talk to your GP or health visitor.

14.vraag: My child is regressing: wetting the bed again, thumb-sucking or clingy with strangers.
14.kort: Regression is a normal reaction to big changes. Your child is seeking safety in familiar behaviour. It usually passes on its own once they feel safe again.
doen: React calmly and don't make a big deal of it.
Give extra closeness and keep routines going.
Tell the other parent what you're seeing, so you both respond the same way.
Praise what is going well.

zeg.samen: It doesn't matter. Everything is new. We're here to help you.
zeg.jong: Never mind. We'll clean it up together. Come here.
zeg.midden: That sometimes happens when a lot is changing. It's not your fault.
zeg.oud: There's no need to be embarrassed. Would you like me to sort something out, or would you rather I didn't?

reageren.kind: "I want to sleep in your bed again."
reageren.jij: "You'd like to be close to me. I'll stay with you until you're asleep, and the door will stay open."

liever: "You're far too big for that."
14.idee: Give your child a small job that feels big, such as laying the table. It builds confidence without pressure.
14.kind: If {kind} isn't laughed at or punished, the regression usually disappears by itself.
14.voorJou: Regression says nothing about your parenting. It shows your child feels safe enough with you to be little.
14.hulp: Has the regression lasted longer than a few months, or is more and more being added to it? Talk to your GP or health visitor.

15.vraag: My child is afraid I'll leave too and clings to me.
15.kort: When one parent moves out, a child can become afraid that the other parent will disappear too. Clinging is a request for certainty. You can give that certainty with words and with predictability.
doen: Always say where you're going and when you'll be back, and keep that promise.
Say goodbye briefly and warmly; don't sneak off.
Build in practice moments: popping out to the shops, being back at the agreed time.
Repeat that parents don't separate from their children.

zeg.samen: Mum and Dad will never leave you. We just live in two homes.
zeg.jong: I'm going to work and I'll pick you up at four o'clock. I always come back.
zeg.midden: Grown-ups can split up, but parents don't leave their children. Ever.
zeg.oud: I understand that makes you scared. I'm staying, and so is Dad/Mum. What would help you feel safer?

reageren.kind: "Are you going to leave too?"
reageren.jij: "No. I'll always be your Mum/Dad. And Dad/Mum too. We will never leave you."

reageren.kind: Your child cries when you go out of the door.
reageren.jij: "I'm going to the shop and I'll be back at three. Look at the clock." And come back on time.

liever: Sneaking off to avoid tears.
"Don't be such a baby."
15.idee: Give your child something small of yours when you leave, such as a scarf or a pebble, to collect again when you come back.
15.kind: Every time you come back as promised, {kind} feels a little more reassured.
15.voorJou: Clinging can wear you out. It passes, by being reliable again and again. You're already doing that.
15.hulp: Is the fear getting worse, is your child sleeping badly or refusing to go to school? Talk to your GP or health visitor.

16.vraag: My child cries over little things or is easily irritable.
16.kort: Sadness about the separation often sits below the surface and comes out over something small: a broken pencil, a lost game. It isn't the pencil, it's everything together.
doen: Comfort them over the small thing, knowing it's about something bigger.
Make sure they get enough sleep, food and rest; being tired makes everything bigger.
Cut down on busyness and stimulation in the weeks after big changes.
At a calm moment, ask whether there's more going on.

zeg.samen: There's just a lot going on at the moment, isn't there? I understand.
zeg.jong: Oh, how sad. Come and sit on my lap for a bit.
zeg.midden: I think there's more to this than the pencil. Do you want to tell me?
zeg.oud: I notice you're on edge. A lot has changed, too. Is there anything I can do?

reageren.kind: Your child bursts into tears over something small.
reageren.jij: "It's all a lot, isn't it?" Comfort first, without explaining.

liever: "Don't make such a fuss, it's only a pencil."
16.idee: Make a list together of things that help when it's all too much: a bath, music, a walk, a cuddle.
16.kind: If {kind} can cry over something small, there's room for the big sadness to come out.
16.voorJou: It takes patience when your child is easily upset. Give yourself breaks too; you don't have to absorb everything.

17.vraag: My child asks why we split up.
17.kort: Be honest, brief and don't blame the other parent. Ideally you both tell the same story. Your child doesn't need details, but does need clarity and reassurance.
doen: Agree with the other parent what you'll say.
Explain that you're no longer in love, not that you no longer care about each other.
Tell them what stays the same for them: school, friends, your love.
Stop if your child loses interest and calmly come back to it later.

zeg.samen: Mum and Dad aren't in love any more. That's why we live apart. We'll always love you just as much.
zeg.jong: Mum and Dad live in two houses now. We'll always love you.
zeg.midden: We're not in love with each other any more and it doesn't work for us to live together in one house. It is never because of you.
zeg.oud: We tried for a long time, but it wasn't working between us any more. The details are ours. You can ask anything you want to know.

reageren.kind: "But you can just fall in love again, can't you?"
reageren.jij: "You'd really like that, wouldn't you? I understand. It's not going to happen. What does stay the same: we're both your parents."

reageren.kind: "Whose idea was it?"
reageren.jij: "That's something between Dad/Mum and me. We decided together and we'll look after you together."

liever: "Ask your father/mother."
Details about arguments, money or a new partner.
17.idee: Read a book about two homes together; there are plenty for every age. It gives words to what your child is feeling.
17.kind: A short story that's the same from both of you gives {kind} peace of mind.
17.voorJou: You don't need the perfect answer. Honest and loving is enough.

18.vraag: My child thinks it's their fault.
18.kort: Many children think they did something wrong: too noisy, too naughty, that one argument. Say it often, even when your child doesn't ask: it's never because of you.
doen: Say it as often as needed, at calm moments.
Ask why your child thinks that, and listen.
Have the other parent say the same thing.
Avoid arguing in front of your child; it feeds the feeling of guilt.

zeg.samen: It's never your fault. Whatever you did or said: this is something between Mum and Dad.
zeg.jong: It's not because of you. Never.
zeg.midden: It really isn't because of you. Not even that time you had an argument. This is about Dad and me.
zeg.oud: This has nothing to do with you, really it doesn't. What makes you think that?

reageren.kind: "If I'd been better behaved, you'd still be together."
reageren.jij: "No, sweetheart. Whatever you had done, it would have turned out the same. This is about Dad and me, never about you."

liever: "If only you'd been a bit better behaved…" (not even as a joke)
Arguing about parenting in front of your child.
18.idee: Have your child draw "what's mine" (friends, hobbies, school) and "what's Mum and Dad's". It helps to place the separation with the parents.
18.kind: {kind} can only let go of it once {kind} has heard it often enough, from both of you.
18.voorJou: It hurts when your child blames themselves. By repeating it again and again, you give your child something they'll carry with them all their life.

19.vraag: My child hopes we'll get back together.
19.kort: That hope is very normal, even after a long time. Be honest and kind: it won't change, and you'll both always be their parents.
doen: Don't give false hope, not even to spare your child.
Acknowledge that your child wishes things were different.
Show what does stay: both of you, in two places.
Be careful about doing things together as a family; it can feed the hope.

zeg.samen: You wish we were together again. I understand. That isn't going to happen. But we'll both always be your parents.
zeg.jong: You want Mum and Dad to live together again. That won't happen. But you have two homes where we love you.
zeg.midden: It's nice when we're both at your birthday, isn't it? Still, we won't get back together. That's sad, and it's OK to feel that.
zeg.oud: I understand you hope for that. I want to be honest: it won't change. What we can do is work together well for you.

reageren.kind: "If I'm really good, will you get back together?"
reageren.jij: "No, sweetheart. It has nothing to do with you. You don't have to do anything. We'll always be your parents."

liever: "Who knows, maybe one day."
19.idee: Keep memories from the past together in a box or album. The past is allowed to be there, even though it won't come back.
19.kind: Honesty helps {kind} to adjust. Lingering hope makes it sad all over again, time after time.
19.voorJou: Perhaps you still feel sad about what's gone too. That's allowed. Find support for it from another adult.

20.vraag: My child asks questions I don't want to or can't answer.
20.kort: About money, arguments, or who did what. You don't have to tell them everything. You can honestly say that some things stay between grown-ups, as long as your child knows they're allowed to ask.
doen: Take the question seriously and thank your child for asking.
Tell them what suits their age; keep adult matters with the adults.
Say when you don't know something, and come back to it later.
Agree with the other parent what you will and won't tell them.

zeg.samen: Good question. Some things are just for Mum and Dad. What we can tell you, we'll tell you honestly.
zeg.jong: That's something for grown-ups. You can ask anything, and I'll tell you what I can.
zeg.midden: That's something between Dad/Mum and me. It has nothing to do with you. Is there something else you'd like to know?
zeg.oud: I want to be honest about this: I'd rather not discuss that with you, because it's between us. That doesn't mean you can't ask.

reageren.kind: "Has Dad/Mum got a girlfriend/boyfriend?"
reageren.jij: "If so, Dad/Mum will tell you himself/herself. That's up to him/her."

reageren.kind: "Do we have less money now?"
reageren.jij: "Some things are changing, but we'll take care of that. You don't need to worry about it."

liever: "You'll have to ask your father/mother, he/she's the one who ruined it."
20.idee: Put out a "question jar": your child writes questions on slips of paper, and you answer them together at a calm moment.
20.kind: {kind} feels taken seriously when questions are welcome, even if not every answer is given.
20.voorJou: Setting limits on what you share protects your child. You're not being dishonest; you're being caring.

21.vraag: My child keeps asking the same thing over and over.
21.kort: Repeating is processing. Children often ask the same thing to get reassurance, or because they've reached a new age and understand it in a new way. Calmly give the same answer every time.
doen: Answer calmly every time, as if it's the first time.
Use the same words each time; it gives them something to hold on to.
Now and then ask back: "What do you think?"

zeg.samen: You asked that before, didn't you? The answer is still the same: we both love you.
zeg.jong: Yes, you have two homes. Mum's/Dad's home and Dad's/Mum's home.
zeg.midden: Good that you're asking again. I'll tell you once more.
zeg.oud: You're still thinking about it a lot, aren't you? What would you like to know about it now?

reageren.kind: "Why did you split up again?" (for the tenth time)
reageren.jij: "We weren't in love any more, and it wasn't working for us together. It's not because of you, and we both love you."

liever: "I've already told you."
21.kind: The same calm answer every time makes {kind}'s world more predictable.
21.voorJou: It can be tiring to keep saying the same thing. Remember: every time, you're building safety.

22.vraag: How do we tell our children?
22.kort: Ideally together, calmly, and at a time when there's room afterwards to recover. Not just before bed or school. Prepare together what you'll say.
doen: Tell them together if you can, and with all the children at the same time.
Choose a calm moment during the day, with time afterwards.
Explain what will actually change: who lives where, what stays the same.
Say that it's not their fault and that you'll both always love them.
Leave room for questions, now and later.

zeg.samen: We want to tell you something important. Mum and Dad are going to separate. We're going to live in two homes. It's not because of you, and we'll both always love you.
zeg.jong: Mum and Dad are going to live in two houses. You'll sometimes live with Mum and sometimes with Dad. We'll both always love you.
zeg.midden: We're separating. That's sad, and it's OK to feel that. You'll keep going to the same school and you'll see both of us.
zeg.oud: We've decided to separate. We know this is a lot for you. You're allowed to be angry or sad, and you can ask anything.

reageren.kind: Your child doesn't react or just goes off to play.
reageren.jij: Let it be. Say: "If you want to ask anything about it later, that's always OK." It often comes later.

reageren.kind: "Where will I live then?"
reageren.jij: Tell them concretely what you know: "During the week you'll live…, and at weekends…" What isn't clear yet, say so honestly.

liever: Telling them just before bedtime.
"We don't love each other any more." (a child may then fear that your love for them will stop too)
22.idee: Agree with the other parent to do something calm with the children after the conversation, such as eating together. It shows: we're still parents.
22.kind: If you tell them together, {kind} sees that you'll keep working together as parents.
22.voorJou: This is one of the hardest conversations. You don't have to do it perfectly. What counts is that you do it together and with love.
22.hulp: Not sure how to approach the conversation? A mediator, your GP or health visitor can help you prepare.

23.vraag: What do I tell the school or childcare?
23.kort: School and childcare see your child every day. If they know what's going on, they can look out for signs and support your child. Briefly explain what's changing, and who picks up when.
doen: Briefly tell the teacher or form tutor that you're separating.
Let them know who picks up when and who should be called.
Ask the school to keep both parents informed about parents' evenings and reports.
Ask them to let you know if they notice anything.

zeg.samen: Your teacher knows that a lot is changing at home. You can tell her/him about it if you want to.
zeg.jong: Your teacher knows you live in two houses now.
zeg.midden: I've told your teacher that we live in two homes, so she/he can help you if you need it. Is that OK?
zeg.oud: I've let your form tutor know what's going on. You decide yourself what else you share.

reageren.kind: "I don't want my teacher to know."
reageren.jij: "I understand. Your teacher won't tell anyone. She just knows, so she can help you if you're having a rotten day."

liever: Using the school to let the other parent know something.
23.kind: If the school knows, {kind} doesn't have to face a rotten day alone.
23.voorJou: Telling the school may feel exposing. You're doing it for your child, and that takes strength.

24.vraag: My child doesn't want to tell anyone or feels ashamed.
24.kort: Some children prefer to keep the separation to themselves. They feel different or don't want it talked about. That's fine. Help your child decide for themselves what they share.
doen: Respect that your child chooses who to tell.
Practise a short sentence together for when friends ask.
Tell them that lots of children live in two homes.

zeg.samen: You decide who you tell. And you know what? There are bound to be other children in your class who live in two homes.
zeg.jong: You can tell people, but you don't have to.
zeg.midden: If someone asks, you can just say: I live with my mum and with my dad. That's all you need to say.
zeg.oud: You decide what you share. Would you like to practise a sentence for when someone asks?

reageren.kind: "Everyone in my class just has one house."
reageren.jij: "It feels like you're the only one, doesn't it? Lots of children have two homes. It's different, not less."

liever: Telling other parents yourself without asking your child.
24.idee: Read a book or watch a series together about a child with two homes. Recognising themselves makes it feel less lonely.
24.kind: If {kind} can decide what to tell, {kind} feels less small.
24.voorJou: Shame in your child isn't a judgement of you. It's a phase of getting used to things.

25.vraag: The first night in the new home.
25.kort: A new home means new sounds, a different bed, different smells. Make it familiar with your child's own things and a familiar bedtime routine.
doen: Set up the room together, with things your child chooses.
Bring familiar things: cuddly toy, duvet, night light.
Keep the bedtime routine exactly the same as always.
Leave the door ajar if your child likes that.

zeg.samen: This is our new home. Your room is yours. What shall we put where?
zeg.jong: Look, your teddy sleeps here too. I'm close by.
zeg.midden: It's still new, isn't it? In a few weeks it'll already feel familiar.
zeg.oud: Set up your room however you like. It's your space.

reageren.kind: "It's scary here."
reageren.jij: "Everything's new, isn't it? I'll stay with you for a bit. Shall we listen together to the sounds this house makes?"

liever: "You'll just have to get used to it."
25.idee: Let your child take a photo of the new home and show it to the other parent. That way the new home becomes part of both parents' story too.
25.kind: A space of their own in the new home means {kind} isn't visiting, but at home.
25.voorJou: A new home is new for you too. Be kind to yourself if it takes a while before it feels like home.

26.vraag: My child doesn't really feel at home anywhere.
26.kort: Two houses only feel like home when your child has a place of their own there and knows what's happening. Predictability is the magic word here.
doen: Give your child a space of their own: a bed, a drawer, something that's theirs.
Use a clear calendar, so your child knows where they'll be when.
Let your child have a say in small things in their room.
Make sure basic things are in both homes.

zeg.samen: This is your home, just like Dad's/Mum's home. What would you like in your room?
zeg.jong: Look, this is where you sleep. Which cuddly toy can go on your bed?
zeg.midden: On the calendar you can see when you're here and when you're at Dad's/Mum's. Shall we put it up together?
zeg.oud: What do you need to feel at home here? You tell me.

reageren.kind: "I never know where I'm going to be."
reageren.jij: "That's hard. Shall we put the calendar up in your room? Then you can always check for yourself."

liever: "You're only here for a few days anyway."
26.idee: Hang the same calendar in both homes, or let your child check in the app where they'll be when.
26.kind: A space of their own in both homes means {kind} isn't always just visiting.
26.voorJou: Building two homes takes time. Small things, like a fixed place for their toothbrush, already make a difference.

27.vraag: The rules are different at the other parent's.
27.kort: Different rules in two homes are normal; children can cope with that well. What matters is that you don't run down each other's rules. A few shared basic rules do help.
doen: Calmly say what the rules are at your place.
Agree a few basic rules with the other parent, such as bedtime on school days and screen time.
Don't let your child play the other parent off against you.

zeg.samen: Maybe that's allowed at Dad's/Mum's. Here we do it like this.
zeg.jong: Here we do it like this.
zeg.midden: Two homes, two ways. This is what we've agreed here.
zeg.oud: I understand it's confusing. These are the rules here. Dad/Mum and I will agree bedtimes together.

reageren.kind: "At Dad's/Mum's I'm allowed on the iPad until ten."
reageren.jij: "Things are different there. Here it's until eight. I will talk to Dad/Mum about it, so it's the same on school days."

liever: "It's always a mess at Dad's/Mum's anyway."
27.idee: Make a list of house rules for your home together with your child. When your child helps decide, it becomes less of a battle.
27.kind: {kind} doesn't have to choose which home is right.
27.voorJou: You have no say over the rules at the other parent's. You do over how you talk about them. That's where you gain the most.

28.vraag: My child keeps forgetting things or doesn't want to take their belongings.
28.kort: Packing your things is also saying goodbye. A fixed list and a fixed place help, as do duplicates of the most important things.
doen: Use the packing list in the app, together with your child.
Have duplicates of the basics: toothbrush, pyjamas, charger.
Let one familiar item always travel with them.
Don't pack at the last minute; do it calmly, the evening before.

zeg.samen: Shall we pack the bag together? Then we won't forget anything.
zeg.jong: Which cuddly toy is coming to Dad's/Mum's?
zeg.midden: Here's your list. Tick off what's in the bag.
zeg.oud: Will you check your list once more? Your charger is in both homes.

reageren.kind: "I don't want to pack."
reageren.jij: "Packing means saying goodbye too, doesn't it? Shall we do it together? It'll be quicker."

liever: "You always forget everything."
28.idee: Make packing cosy: a regular song to go with it, or packing the bag together on the same evening each time.
28.kind: If packing goes calmly, the handover is already a lot easier for {kind}.
28.voorJou: Forgotten things can lead to hassle between parents. A list and duplicate items save a lot of arguments.

29.vraag: Saying goodbye at the handover is hard.
29.kort: Saying goodbye is often the hardest moment for children, more so than the other parent themselves. Short, warm and predictable works best. Lingering makes it harder.
doen: Create a short, fixed goodbye ritual: a hug, a phrase, a wave.
Don't show your own sadness at that moment; that can come later.
Speak positively about the time at the other parent's.
Is there tension between you? Then do the handover via school or childcare.

zeg.samen: Have a lovely time at Dad's/Mum's! See you on Sunday. Big hug.
zeg.jong: Hug! Have a lovely time. After three sleeps you'll be back here.
zeg.midden: Have fun! I'm looking forward to Sunday.
zeg.oud: Have a good time. Message me if you like.

reageren.kind: Your child clings on at the door.
reageren.jij: Give a hug, say your usual phrase, and calmly hand your child over. Don't leave them hanging in doubt.

reageren.kind: "I want to stay with you."
reageren.jij: "I know, goodbyes are hard. Dad/Mum is looking forward to seeing you. You'll be back here on Sunday."

liever: "I'm going to miss you sooo much."
Carrying on talking at the door.
29.idee: Come up with a secret goodbye together: a special handshake or phrase that's just yours.
29.kind: A short, warm goodbye lets {kind} go to the other parent with peace of mind.
29.voorJou: Letting your child go when it's hard asks a lot of you. You do it for your child, and that's love.

30.vraag: My child comes back and says nothing, or tells me everything.
30.kort: Some children need time to land and only talk later. Others tell you everything straight away. Both are normal. Listen without judging and don't probe about the other parent.
doen: Give your child time; stories often come out at dinner or in bed.
Respond neutrally or positively to stories about the other parent.
Don't probe about the other parent or his or her new life.

zeg.samen: Lovely to have you back. Tell me whenever you like.
zeg.jong: Did you have fun playing at Dad's/Mum's?
zeg.midden: You don't have to tell me anything. But I'd love to hear if you want to.
zeg.oud: Welcome back. All good?

reageren.kind: Your child tells you about something you don't approve of.
reageren.jij: "Oh, so that's how it went there." Stay calm. Want to discuss it? Do that later with the other parent, not with your child.

liever: "So, what did Dad/Mum get up to? Was that girlfriend there?"
30.kind: If {kind} isn't interrogated, {kind} will dare to tell you things of their own accord.
30.voorJou: Curiosity about the other home is human. Protecting your child from being questioned is a big thing.

31.vraag: My teenager wants to spend more or less time with the other parent.
31.kort: Teenagers increasingly have a life of their own: friends, sport, a part-time job. Their wishes about the arrangement change. Listen seriously, but don't let them choose alone. It remains an agreement between parents.
doen: Ask about the reason behind the wish.
Discuss it with the other parent, without putting pressure on your teenager.
Look for a solution that fits your teenager's life.
Let your teenager know that their opinion counts, and that you decide together.

zeg.samen: What you want matters. Dad/Mum and I will talk it over, and we'll let you know what we agree.
zeg.jong: Dad/Mum and I will work out together what's best.
zeg.midden: Good that you've told me. Dad/Mum and I are going to talk about it.
zeg.oud: I'm glad you've told me. What's going on? I'll discuss it with Dad/Mum, and we'll take what you want seriously.

reageren.kind: "I want to be at Dad's/Mum's more, that's where my friends are."
reageren.jij: "I understand. Your friends are important. I'll look with Dad/Mum at what's possible."

reageren.kind: "I don't want to go to Dad's/Mum's every weekend any more."
reageren.jij: "What makes it difficult? Tell me. We'll look for a solution together with Dad/Mum."

liever: "You can choose for yourself." (that puts the burden on your child)
"Well, you'll have to tell Dad/Mum that yourself."
31.kind: {kind} feels heard when the wish is taken seriously, and protected when the decision stays with you.
31.voorJou: It can hurt when your teenager wants to be with you less. Often it's about your teenager's own life, not about you.
31.hulp: Can't work it out together? A mediator can help. In the Netherlands, children aged 12 and over can also give their own view to the judge.

32.vraag: There's a new partner, mine or the other parent's.
32.kort: A new partner is a big deal for children: it makes the separation final and stirs up loyalty. Take your time, tell them yourself, and let your child set their own pace.
doen: Tell them yourself, before your child hears it somewhere else.
Don't let the new partner take on a parenting role, certainly not at the start.
Keep first meetings short and in a neutral place.
Keep some time alone with your child, without the new partner.
Is it the other parent's partner? Show that your child is allowed to like that person.

zeg.samen: I've met someone I like. You're still the most important people in the world to me.
zeg.jong: This is Mark. He's a friend of Mum's/Dad's. You're still my very favourite.
zeg.midden: I want to tell you something: I've met someone. You can ask anything, and you don't have to like him/her straight away.
zeg.oud: I'd rather tell you myself. I've met someone. How do you feel about that?

reageren.kind: "He/she is not my dad/mum!"
reageren.jij: "That's absolutely right. You have a dad and a mum. Mark is a friend of mine, nothing more."

reageren.kind: "Am I allowed to like Dad's girlfriend?"
reageren.jij: "Of course! I'm glad for you."

liever: "This is your new dad/mum."
"I hope you don't like her/him more than me."
32.idee: Plan a regular time alone with your child, for example breakfast together on Saturday mornings. It shows your bond isn't changing.
32.kind: {kind} can like the new partner without being disloyal to either of you.
32.voorJou: The other parent's new partner can stir up a lot. That's allowed. Don't let your child carry the weight of it.

33.vraag: My child has to get used to the new partner's children.
33.kort: Suddenly sharing with other children: space, attention, sometimes a bedroom. That's a lot. Go slowly, give each child their own space and don't expect them to be brothers and sisters straight away.
doen: Give each child a space of their own, however small.
Plan separate time with your own child.
Agree a few house rules together that apply to everyone.
Don't expect friendship; respect is enough.

zeg.samen: You don't have to be friends straight away. But do be kind to each other.
zeg.jong: This is your shelf, nobody else touches it.
zeg.midden: It takes getting used to, doesn't it, other children in the house? What do you find hardest?
zeg.oud: I understand you sometimes just want to be alone. Your room is your space.

reageren.kind: "He/she gets everything and I get nothing."
reageren.jij: "That's how it feels to you. What would you like? Let's plan something together, just you and me."

liever: "Oh, just be nice and join in."
33.kind: {kind} needs time. Their own space and time with you make getting used to it easier.
33.voorJou: A blended family asks patience of everyone, including you. It grows step by step.
33.hulp: Do things keep getting stuck at home? Family coaching can help; ask your GP or local family support services.

34.vraag: My child is unkind to the new partner, or doesn't want to see him or her.
34.kort: Rejection is often loyalty: your child doesn't want to betray the other parent. Don't force anything. Give it time, while still holding on to normal good manners.
doen: Name the feeling and the loyalty that may be behind it.
Don't ask your child for things they're not ready for, like hugging or going out together.
Do agree that everyone treats each other politely.
Ask the new partner to be patient and not take on a parenting role.

zeg.samen: You don't have to like him/her. But you do need to be polite.
zeg.jong: You don't have to sit on Mark's lap. Saying hello is enough.
zeg.midden: I can see you find it hard that Mark is here. I understand. Do you want to tell me what's hard about it?
zeg.oud: You don't have to get used to it straight away. I'm only asking you to behave normally. What would make it easier?

reageren.kind: "If I like him/her, Dad/Mum will be sad."
reageren.jij: "That's so kind of you to think of Dad/Mum. You're allowed to like anyone. Dad/Mum will always be your Dad/Mum."

liever: "Stop being so difficult with Mark."
Forcing your child to go out together.
34.idee: Let the new partner do something your child enjoys, without any pressure: setting out a game, cooking together if your child wants to.
34.kind: {kind} may be protecting the other parent. Space and patience help more than pushing.
34.voorJou: It's painful when your child rejects your new partner. It's almost always about loyalty, not about your choice.

35.vraag: A half-brother or half-sister is on the way.
35.kort: A new baby for one of the parents can bring joy, but also the question: do I still belong? Tell them in good time and let your child have a role of their own.
doen: Tell them yourself and in good time, before it shows or others mention it.
Emphasise that your child keeps their place.
Give your child a role, if they want one: helping think of a name, choosing a present.
Keep regular time alone with your child.

zeg.samen: A baby is coming. You're going to be a big brother or sister. You'll stay just as important to us.
zeg.jong: A baby is coming. You'll always be my big child.
zeg.midden: You're getting a half-brother or half-sister. How do you feel about that? Whatever you feel is OK.
zeg.oud: I wanted to tell you myself. Your place with us won't change. How do you feel about it?

reageren.kind: "Will you love the baby more then?"
reageren.jij: "No. Love doesn't get smaller when someone new arrives. You'll stay just as important."

liever: "Now we'll finally be a real family."
35.kind: Above all, {kind} wants to know: do I still belong? Say it often.
35.voorJou: If it's the other parent's baby, that can stir up a lot. Let your child be happy about it.

36.kort: On special days children feel the difference most strongly. Clear arrangements and a tradition of your own help. Celebrating twice can simply be fun, too.
doen: Agree well in advance with the other parent who celebrates when.
Create your own tradition on your day, even if it doesn't fall on the actual date.
Let your child make or buy something for the other parent.
Ask your child what they would like.

zeg.samen: On Christmas Eve you're at Dad's/Mum's, and we'll celebrate the day after. Then you get two celebrations!
zeg.jong: We'll have another party, just the two of us. What would you like to eat?
zeg.midden: We'll celebrate your birthday twice: here and at Dad's/Mum's. What would you like to do here?
zeg.oud: How would you like to do it this year? We'll see together what's possible.

reageren.kind: "Why can't we all just be together?"
reageren.jij: "You wish we could be together, don't you? I understand. We celebrate in two places now, with just as much love."

liever: "I'll be all on my own then."
36.idee: Come up with a tradition that belongs just to you: a Christmas breakfast on 27 December, a birthday cake you bake together.
36.kind: If {kind} doesn't have to choose where the celebration is best, {kind} can simply enjoy it.
36.voorJou: Holidays without your child can be lonely. Plan something for yourself and spend time with people you care about.

37.kort: A day to celebrate the other parent can feel awkward. Help your child make or give something anyway. In doing so you give your child a big gift: permission to love you both.
doen: Help your child make a present or drawing for the other parent.
Agree that your child is with that parent on that day.
Is it made at school while they're staying with you? Let them take it along happily.

zeg.samen: It's Father's Day on Sunday. Shall we make something for Dad together?
zeg.jong: Shall we make a drawing for Dad?
zeg.midden: It's Father's Day on Sunday. What do you think Dad would like?
zeg.oud: It's Father's Day on Sunday. Would you like to sort something out for Dad? I'm happy to help.

reageren.kind: "Can I give this to Dad?"
reageren.jij: "Of course. He/she is going to love it."

liever: "He/she never does that for me either."
37.kind: When you help with a present for the other parent, {kind} feels free to love you both.
37.voorJou: Helping make a present for the other parent takes generosity. Your child notices, even if they don't say so.

38.vraag: My child is going on a long holiday with the other parent.
38.kort: Two or three weeks away is a long time for children and parents. A few arrangements about contact and a good goodbye make it lighter for everyone.
doen: Agree with the other parent how often there will be contact, for example two video calls a week.
Give your child something to send to you: a postcard or photo.
Show that you're happy for your child.
Plan something nice for yourself during those weeks.

zeg.samen: Have a lovely holiday! Shall we video call on Sunday? Will you send me a photo of the beach?
zeg.jong: Have a lovely holiday! Take your cuddly toy. We'll give each other a call.
zeg.midden: I can't wait to hear your stories. Shall we video call on Sunday evening?
zeg.oud: Enjoy it. Send me a photo if you feel like it.

reageren.kind: "Won't you miss me?"
reageren.jij: "Yes, I will, and that's OK. I'm glad you're having a lovely holiday. I'll see you when you get back."

liever: "Three weeks is a very long time without me."
38.idee: Make a countdown calendar to their return together, or give them a sealed envelope to open halfway through.
38.kind: If you let {kind} go with peace of mind, {kind} can really enjoy the holiday.
38.voorJou: Weeks without your child can feel quiet. Fill them with things that do you good. Your child will come back.

39.vraag: School events we both attend: reports, the school play, sports day.
39.kort: For your child, the best thing is when you're both there and it's calm. You don't have to stand side by side; a friendly hello is enough.
doen: Agree beforehand who stands or sits where, if that keeps things calm.
Greet each other kindly in front of your child.
Keep difficult topics away from this moment.
Both arrive on time and don't leave without seeing your child.

zeg.samen: You did so well! We're both here.
zeg.jong: Mum and Dad are both watching you!
zeg.midden: How lovely that we were both there. You did so well.
zeg.oud: We're proud of you, both of us.

reageren.kind: Your child is looking back and forth between you.
reageren.jij: Both give a wave, and give each other a nod. Your child sees that it's safe.

liever: Arguing with the other parent in the playground.
39.kind: {kind} sees that you're both there and that it's calm. That's the best gift of all.
39.voorJou: Being somewhere together can feel tense. A smile and a hello are enough. You're doing it for your child.

40.vraag: I miss my child when they're with the other parent.
40.kort: You're allowed to miss your child too. Your child doesn't have to carry that. Use the time to recharge, so you're fully there again when your child comes back.
doen: Let your child know you're glad they're going to the other parent.
Plan something for yourself on handover day.
Feel free to send a short message, but don't keep asking how it's going.
Spend time with people who give you energy.

zeg.samen: Have a lovely time at Dad's/Mum's! See you on Sunday.
zeg.jong: Have a lovely time! After three sleeps you'll be back here.
zeg.midden: Have fun at Dad's/Mum's. I'm looking forward to Sunday.
zeg.oud: Have a good time. Message me if you like, you don't have to.

reageren.kind: "What are you going to do while I'm away?"
reageren.jij: "I'm going for a walk with a friend and having a good read. I'll be absolutely fine. You enjoy yourself."

liever: "I'm going to miss you sooo much, it'll be so quiet here."
40.idee: Make a list of things you'll do while your child is away: exercise, see friends, learn something new. Look at it when it feels quiet.
40.kind: If you let {kind} go with peace of mind, {kind} can be at the other parent's with peace of mind too.
40.voorJou: Missing them is part of it. You're no less a parent when your child isn't there. Take good care of yourself; that's also taking care of your child.
40.hulp: Do you find the missing hard to bear? Talk about it with someone you trust, or with your GP. You can always talk it through with Co too.

41.vraag: I feel guilty towards my child.
41.kort: Almost every separated parent feels guilty at times. Children don't need perfect parents; they need parents who are there, are honest and work well together. You can contribute to that every day.
doen: Be kind to yourself: you're doing what you can.
Don't compensate with presents or fewer rules; predictability helps your child more.
Focus on what you can do now: being there, listening, working together.
Talk about your guilt with an adult, not with your child.

zeg.samen: I'm here for you, always.
zeg.jong: I love you, always.
zeg.midden: I know it's not easy for you. I'm here for you.
zeg.oud: I'm sorry it's so hard for you. I'm doing my best, and I want to hear it if something could be better.

reageren.kind: "You two ruined everything."
reageren.jij: "I understand it feels that way. It's really hard for you. I'm here, and I'll keep doing my best."

liever: "I'm so sorry, I'm a terrible parent." (that puts the burden on your child)
41.idee: Every evening, write down one thing that went well with your child. After a few weeks you'll see how much you do.
41.kind: {kind} doesn't need a perfect parent, just a parent who is there.
41.voorJou: Guilt looks backwards. Your child gets more from what you do today. And you're already doing it.
41.hulp: Is the guilt still weighing heavily? Talk about it with your GP or a psychologist. Taking good care of yourself is good for your child too.

42.vraag: I'm angry with the other parent and my child notices.
42.kort: Your anger may be completely justified. Still, children pick up tension between parents unerringly, and it can cause worry, poor sleep and stress. You're allowed to be angry; your child doesn't have to carry it.
doen: Talk about your anger with adults, not in front of your child.
Use Write it out or Breathe in the app at difficult moments.
Does your child notice anyway? Say that it isn't about him or her.
Look at what's within your control: your tone, your reaction.

zeg.samen: You can tell I'm angry. That's something between Mum and Dad. It's not about you.
zeg.jong: Mum/Dad is a bit cross right now. Not with you.
zeg.midden: I was angry on the phone just now. That wasn't about you, and you don't need to do anything about it.
zeg.oud: You noticed I was angry. I'll sort that out with Dad/Mum myself. Sorry you heard it.

reageren.kind: "Why are you always angry with Dad/Mum?"
reageren.jij: "Sometimes we don't agree. We'll sort that out. You're allowed to love Dad/Mum, and I think that's good."

liever: "Your father/mother is truly impossible."
Arguing on the phone while your child is listening.
42.idee: Make a pact with yourself: you only have difficult conversations with the other parent when your child isn't around. Schedule them if you need to.
42.kind: {kind} is happiest when they can see there's no tension between Mum and Dad.
42.voorJou: You're allowed to be angry. By keeping it out of your child's sight, you protect your child from a burden that isn't theirs.
42.hulp: Does the tension between you keep building? A mediator or parenting coach can help. If you're worried about safety in the Netherlands: Veilig Thuis, 0800-2000.

43.vraag: I don't know if my child is coming to terms with the separation.
43.kort: Every child processes a separation in their own way and at their own pace. Most children adjust well within one to two years, especially when parents argue little and the child is allowed to love them both.
doen: Look out for signs: sleep, eating, school, friends, mood.
Ask school or childcare how things are going there.
Compare notes with the other parent on what you're both seeing.
Keep talking and listening, even when things seem to be going well.

zeg.samen: How are you actually doing? Really?
zeg.jong: Are you happy or sad today? Point to it.
zeg.midden: What was the best thing about today? And the worst?
zeg.oud: How are you really doing? You can tell me, even if it's not going well.

reageren.kind: "It's fine."
reageren.jij: "OK. If there's a time it isn't, you can always tell me. I won't mind."

liever: "You're doing fine, aren't you?"
43.idee: Set a regular time each week to really be together: walking, cycling, cooking together. Children talk most when they're busy next to you.
43.kind: {kind} notices that you're paying attention. That builds trust, even if {kind} doesn't say much.
43.voorJou: The fact that you're asking this question shows how involved you are. Trust what you see.
43.hulp: Sleeping badly, withdrawing, lots of anger, poor school results for more than a few months, or talking about not wanting to live any more? Go to your GP straight away. In the Netherlands, children can also call the Kindertelefoon themselves: 0800-0432.
